arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Katz stated that only two ways exist to vacate an award under the applicable standard.
Mr. Waxman cited Stolt-Nielsen to argue that arbitration requires a clear contractual basis.
Justice Ginsburg noted that arbitrators interpret contract terms and courts rarely overturn them.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests the limits of judicial review over arbitration awards. Oxford Health Plans argues the arbitrator distorted facts. Sutter argues courts must defer to arbitrators on factual matters.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on March 25, 2013.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Oxford Health Plans wants the Court to allow courts to vacate awards based on factual errors.
Sutter wants the Court to bar courts from reviewing arbitrators' factual findings.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Oxford Health Plans argues that severe factual distortion transforms a fact issue into a legal one.
Sutter argues that arbitrators decide facts and courts cannot second-guess those decisions.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked if factual distortion becomes a legal question at some point.
Justice Sotomayor asked if this is always an arbitrator's question or a mistake here.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between judicial review and arbitration finality. It determines whether courts can correct factual errors in private dispute resolution. The outcome shapes the reliability of arbitration as a legal mechanism.
